hero.title: What is Islamic Finance?
hero.subtitle: A comprehensive introduction to Shariah-compliant banking, core principles, and how Islamic finance operates across different regulatory environments.

introduction.leadParagraph: Islamic finance is a financial system based on principles derived from Islamic law (Shariah), which prohibits interest (riba) and promotes ethical, asset-backed transactions with risk-sharing mechanisms.
introduction.paragraph1: Unlike conventional banking, which relies heavily on interest-based lending and debt instruments, Islamic finance emphasizes partnerships, trade, and shared accountability between financial institutions and their customers. This approach aligns financial activities with Islamic ethical and moral values, ensuring that all transactions are transparent, fair, and beneficial to society.
introduction.paragraph2: Across regions like West and Central Africa (including CEMAC and WAEMU) as well as Nigeria (under the CBN), Islamic finance is growing rapidly as institutions seek alternatives to conventional banking that better serve diverse populations while remaining compliant with regional banking regulations and international accounting frameworks.

corePrinciples.title: Core Principles of Islamic Finance
corePrinciples.intro: Islamic finance is built on five fundamental principles that distinguish it from conventional financial systems:

ribaProhibition.title: Prohibition of Riba (Interest)
ribaProhibition.description: All forms of interest whether fixed or variable are strictly prohibited. Money must not generate money on its own.

riskSharing.title: Risk-Sharing
riskSharing.description: Profits and losses must be shared between parties. No party bears all the risk alone.

assetBacked.title: Asset-Backed Transactions
assetBacked.description: Every financial transaction must be backed by a tangible asset or service. Speculation is discouraged.

ethicalInvestment.title: Ethical Investment
ethicalInvestment.description: Investments in prohibited sectors (alcohol, gambling, pork, weapons) are not allowed.

transparency.title: Transparency
transparency.description: All contracts must be clear, unambiguous, and free from uncertainty (gharar).

prohibitionRiba.title: Prohibition of Riba (Interest)
prohibitionRiba.intro: The most fundamental principle in Islamic finance is the prohibition of riba, commonly translated as "interest" or "usury." In the Islamic tradition, riba represents any guaranteed increase on a loan or debt, regardless of the percentage.

whyProhibited.title: Why is Interest Prohibited?
whyProhibited.intro: Islamic scholars argue that interest-based lending creates an unjust economic system where:

reasons.riskUnbalanced: Risk is unbalanced: The lender receives guaranteed returns without bearing any risk, while the borrower assumes all the risk.
reasons.exploitation: Exploitation occurs: Interest compounds over time, potentially trapping borrowers in cycles of debt.
reasons.moneyCommodity: Money becomes a commodity: Interest allows money to generate more money without productive economic activity.
reasons.socialInequality: Social inequality grows: Wealth concentrates among lenders while borrowers struggle with debt burdens.

replacement.title: What Replaces Interest?
replacement.intro: Instead of interest, Islamic finance uses profit-sharing arrangements where returns are tied to the performance of actual business activities or investments. For example:

examples.murabaha: Murabaha (cost-plus sale): The bank purchases an asset and resells it to the customer at a marked-up price, disclosed upfront.
examples.mudarabah: Mudarabah (profit-sharing): The bank provides capital, and the entrepreneur provides expertise. Profits are shared according to a pre-agreed ratio.
examples.musharakah: Musharakah (partnership): Both parties contribute capital and share profits and losses proportionally.

riskSharing.title: Risk-Sharing & Profit-Loss Sharing
riskSharing.intro: Islamic finance promotes shared accountability. Both the financial institution and the customer must participate in the risks and rewards of a transaction.

items.fairness: Fairness: No party can earn a return without accepting some level of risk.
items.stability: Economic stability: Risk-sharing discourages excessive leverage and speculative bubbles.
items.alignment: Alignment of interests: The bank and the customer work together toward mutual success rather than being adversaries.

example.title: Practical Example: Mudarabah Investment Account
example.description: A customer deposits 10 million FCFA into a Mudarabah savings account. The bank (acting as mudarib or fund manager) invests this capital in Shariah-compliant ventures.
example.profitScenario: If the investments generate a profit of 500,000 FCFA, the profit is split according to a Profit-Sharing Ratio (PSR)—say 60% to the customer and 40% to the bank.
example.lossScenario: If the investments result in a loss due to market conditions (not negligence), the customer bears the loss on capital, and the bank loses its time and effort.
example.comparison: This is fundamentally different from conventional savings accounts, where the bank guarantees a fixed interest rate regardless of its investment performance.

assetBacked.title: Asset-Backed Transactions
assetBacked.intro: Every Islamic financial transaction must be backed by a tangible asset, service, or economic activity. This principle ensures that financial transactions contribute to real economic growth rather than speculative bubbles.

items.prevention: Prevents speculation: Money cannot be lent for its own sake. It must be tied to something productive.
items.reducesRisk: Reduces systemic risk: Asset-backed finance is more stable than derivative-heavy conventional finance.
items.encourages: Encourages productive investment: Capital flows to sectors that generate real goods and services.

items.murabaha: Murabaha for equipment purchase: A microfinance institution buys a sewing machine for a tailor and sells it to them at cost + markup.
items.ijara: Ijara for vehicle leasing: The bank owns the vehicle and leases it to the customer, who eventually purchases it.
items.salam: Salam for agricultural financing: The bank pre-purchases a farmer's crop at a discounted price, providing immediate capital.

ethicalInvestment.intro: Islamic finance institutions are prohibited from investing in sectors that are haram (forbidden) under Shariah. This creates an ethical investment framework that excludes:

positive.intro: Beyond sector exclusions, Islamic finance also emphasizes positive social impact, encouraging investments in:

regulatoryContext.title: Regulatory & Regional Frameworks

items.cbn: CBN Guidelines (Nigeria): The Central Bank of Nigeria has established frameworks for non-interest banking windows, full non-interest bank operations, and regulatory segregation of general ledgers.
items.cemac: COBAC & BEAC (Central Africa / CEMAC): Microfinance institutions and banks follow directives set by the Central African Banking Commission and monetary policies by the Bank of Central African States.

hero.title: Understanding Murabaha Financing
hero.subtitle: A step-by-step breakdown of how cost-plus sale financing works in Islamic banking, from contract structure to pricing mechanisms.

introduction.leadParagraph: Murabaha (also spelled Murabahah) is the most widely used Islamic financing structure, accounting for approximately 70% of all Islamic banking transactions worldwide. It's a cost-plus sale arrangement where the bank purchases an asset and resells it to the customer at a disclosed markup.
introduction.paragraph1: The term "Murabaha" comes from the Arabic word ribh (profit), and literally means "a sale on mutually agreed profit." Unlike conventional interest-based loans, Murabaha is a trade transaction involving the purchase and sale of a tangible asset not the lending of money.
introduction.paragraph2: Across different regulatory jurisdictions, Murabaha is particularly popular for:

howItWorks.title: How Murabaha Works
howItWorks.intro: Murabaha transforms what would be a conventional loan into a Shariah-compliant sale transaction. Here's the fundamental structure:

step1.title: Customer identifies a need:
step1.description: The customer wants to acquire an asset (e.g., a delivery truck) but lacks immediate capital.

step2.title: Promise to purchase:
step2.description: The customer promises to buy the asset from the bank once the bank acquires it (this promise is binding in most jurisdictions).

step3.title: Bank purchases the asset:
step3.description: The bank buys the asset from a supplier using its own funds.

step4.title: Bank takes ownership:
step4.description: The asset is legally owned by the bank, even if briefly.

step5.title: Bank sells to customer:
step5.description: The bank resells the asset to the customer at cost + markup, fully disclosed.

step6.title: Deferred payment:
step6.description: The customer pays the total price in installments over an agreed period.

howItWorks.keyDistinction: The key distinction from a conventional loan is that the bank owns the asset before selling it, making this a genuine trade transaction rather than a debt instrument with interest.

transactionFlow.title: Murabaha Transaction Flow
transactionFlow.intro: Let's walk through a concrete example: a microenterprise in Douala, Cameroon, needs a 5 million FCFA sewing machine to expand production.

step1.title: Customer Application
step1.description: The tailor approaches an Islamic microfinance institution (MFI) and requests Murabaha financing for a specific sewing machine model from a local supplier.

step2.title: Promise to Purchase
step2.description: The customer signs a binding promise to purchase the sewing machine once the bank acquires it. This promise includes the agreed markup percentage (e.g., 15% over 24 months).

step3.title: Bank Purchases Asset
step3.description: The bank buys the sewing machine directly from the supplier for 5 million FCFA. The bank pays cash and obtains full legal ownership.

step4.title: Ownership Transfer
step4.description: The bank takes delivery of the sewing machine. Even if this ownership is brief, it's legally documented (purchase invoice, ownership certificate).

step5.title: Sale to Customer
step5.description: The bank sells the sewing machine to the customer for 5,750,000 FCFA (5M cost + 750K markup = 15% profit). The contract specifies 24 monthly installments of 239,583 FCFA.

step6.title: Installment Payments
step6.description: The customer pays 239,583 FCFA monthly for 24 months. The total price is fixed and cannot change (unlike variable-rate conventional loans).

pricing.title: Pricing & Markup Calculation
pricing.intro: One of the most important aspects of Murabaha is transparent pricing. The bank must disclose:

disclosureItems.cost: The original cost of the asset

howDetermined.title: How Markup is Determined
howDetermined.intro: While the markup percentage is not technically "interest," it serves a similar economic function. Islamic scholars permit profit on trade transactions, and banks consider several factors when setting the markup:

factors.market: Market rates: Competitive pricing compared to conventional financing options
factors.risk: Risk assessment: Customer creditworthiness and asset quality
factors.period: Financing period: Longer terms typically command higher markups
factors.asset: Asset type: Liquid assets (easily resold) may have lower markups
factors.admin: Administrative costs: Operational expenses of executing the transaction

example.title: Murabaha Pricing Example
example.note: Note: The total price is fixed at contract signing. Unlike conventional loans with variable interest rates, Murabaha prices cannot change.

fixedVsVariable.title: Fixed vs Variable Pricing
fixedVsVariable.intro: A critical Shariah requirement: once the Murabaha contract is signed, the price is immutable. This differs significantly from conventional loans where interest rates can fluctuate.
fixedVsVariable.conventional: Conventional loan: Principal + variable interest rate (can increase/decrease)
fixedVsVariable.murabaha: Murabaha: Fixed selling price (cost + markup), disclosed upfront and unchangeable

documentation.title: Required Documentation
documentation.intro: Proper Murabaha execution requires comprehensive documentation to ensure Shariah compliance and legal enforceability:

items.application: Murabaha financing application: Details of the asset needed and financing amount
items.promise: Promise to purchase (wa'ad): Binding commitment to buy the asset once the bank acquires it
items.agency: Agency agreement (optional): In some cases, the customer acts as the bank's agent to purchase the asset on the bank's behalf
items.contract: Murabaha sale contract: The final sale agreement specifying cost, markup, total price, and payment terms
items.collateral: Collateral documentation: Security agreements, guarantees, or asset pledges

items.invoice: Purchase invoice from supplier: Proof that the bank acquired the asset
items.ownership: Ownership certificate: Evidence that the bank legally owned the asset before reselling it
items.shariah: Shariah board approval: Confirmation that the product structure complies with Islamic law
items.regulatory: Regulatory compliance checklist: Verification that the transaction meets local banking or microfinance regulations
items.risk: Internal risk assessment: Credit evaluation and approval documentation

bestPractice.title: Documentation Best Practice
bestPractice.description: Many Islamic finance institutions streamline the process by creating a Master Murabaha Framework Agreement that covers general terms, then use simple purchase orders for individual transactions. This reduces paperwork while maintaining Shariah compliance.

vsConventional.title: Murabaha vs Conventional Loan
vsConventional.intro: While Murabaha and conventional loans may appear similar economically, they differ fundamentally in structure and philosophy:

useCases.title: Common Use Cases
useCases.intro: Murabaha is highly versatile and is widely used across various markets for business and consumer financing:

workingCapital.title: Working Capital Financing
workingCapital.example: A textile trader needs 20 million local currency units (e.g. FCFA or Naira) to purchase fabric inventory from a regional supplier.

points.point1: The bank purchases the fabric from the supplier
points.point2: The bank sells the fabric to the trader at cost + 12% markup
points.point3: The trader pays in 6 monthly installments as they sell the fabric to retailers

equipment.title: Equipment Acquisition
equipment.example: A construction company needs a cement mixer worth 8 million units.

points.point1: The bank buys the cement mixer from the equipment supplier
points.point2: The bank sells it to the company at cost + 18% markup over 36 months
points.point3: The company makes monthly payments according to the fixed installment schedule

vehicle.title: Vehicle Financing
vehicle.example: A delivery service needs three motorcycles totaling 6 million units.

points.point1: The bank purchases the motorcycles from a local dealer
points.point2: The bank resells them at cost + 20% markup over 18 months
points.point3: Fixed monthly installments are set at contract signing

import.title: Import Finance
import.example: An electronics retailer wants to import smartphones worth 50 million units.

points.point1: The bank purchases the smartphones on behalf of the retailer
points.point2: The bank sells them to the retailer at cost + 10% markup

compliance.title: Regulatory Compliance
compliance.intro: Islamic finance institutions must navigate both Shariah requirements and local banking regulations across different jurisdictions:

items.licensing: Licensing: Must obtain appropriate banking authorizations or non-interest window approvals from local regulators (like CBN in Nigeria, COBAC in CEMAC, or BCEAO in WAEMU).
items.capital: Capital adequacy: Compliance with capital adequacy guidelines and liquidity ratios specified by regional or national guidelines.
items.reporting: Reporting: Regular submission of compliant financial reports and returns to central bank auditors.
items.classification: Asset classification: Murabaha receivables must be properly classified and provisioned per local regulatory frameworks.
items.exposure: Maximum financing exposure: Strict caps on single-obligor exposure limits.

items.recognition: Asset recognition: The bank must record the asset on its balance sheet when purchased.
items.revenue: Revenue recognition: Markup can be recognized over the financing period (accrual basis) or at sale (cash basis), depending on local accounting policies.
items.disclosure: Disclosure requirements: Audit notes must clearly explain the nature of Murabaha transactions.

items.ace: ACE (Advisory Committee of Experts): Establish a Shariah supervisory board to approve product structures.
items.review: Pre-transaction review: Each Murabaha contract should be reviewed for Shariah compliance.
items.audit: Annual Shariah audit: Independent review of all Islamic transactions.
items.fatwa: Fatwa documentation: Written Shariah opinions justifying product structures.

risks.title: Risks & Mitigation Strategies
risks.intro: While Murabaha is relatively straightforward, several risks require careful management:

commodity.title: Commodity Risk
commodity.risk: The bank briefly owns the asset before selling it to the customer. If the asset is damaged, lost, or devalues during this period, the bank bears the loss.

strategies.minimize: Minimize the ownership period (ideally same-day transaction)
strategies.insurance: Obtain insurance on the asset during ownership
strategies.inspection: Conduct thorough asset inspections before purchase
strategies.agency: Use agency agreements where the customer acts as the bank's purchasing agent

credit.title: Credit Risk
credit.risk: The customer may default on installment payments.

strategies.diversification: Diversification across multiple customers and sectors
strategies.monitoring: Regular monitoring of customer financial health

shariahNonCompliance.title: Shariah Non-Compliance Risk
shariahNonCompliance.risk: Improper documentation or execution could render the transaction non-Shariah compliant.

legal.title: Legal Risk
legal.risk: Local legal systems in some jurisdictions may not fully recognize Islamic finance structures, complicating enforcement.

strategies.experts: Work with legal experts familiar with both local commercial laws (e.g. OHADA) and Islamic finance
strategies.clarifications: Obtain regulatory clarifications on non-interest product treatment
strategies.language: Use clear, legally enforceable contract language
strategies.documentation: Maintain thorough documentation for all transactions

hero.title: Profit-Sharing Ratio Disclosure
hero.subtitle: How to properly disclose Profit-Sharing Ratios (PSR) to customers in Mudarabah investment accounts while meeting Shariah and regulatory requirements.

introduction.leadParagraph: The Profit-Sharing Ratio (PSR) is the predetermined percentage split of profits earned from Mudarabah investment accounts the most common Islamic alternative to conventional interest-bearing savings accounts.
introduction.paragraph1: In a Mudarabah arrangement, the customer (rab al-mal, or capital provider) deposits funds into an investment account, and the bank (mudarib, or fund manager) invests those funds in Shariah-compliant ventures. When profits are generated, they are distributed according to the PSR agreed upon at the start of the relationship.
introduction.paragraph2: For example, a PSR of 60:40 means:

customer.text: of profits go to the customer (depositor)

bank.text: of profits go to the bank (investment manager)

introduction.paragraph3: Unlike conventional interest rates, which are fixed and guaranteed, PSR-based returns fluctuate based on actual investment performance. This aligns with Islamic principles of risk-sharing and profit-loss distribution.

whyMatters.title: Why PSR Disclosure Matters
whyMatters.intro: Transparent disclosure of Profit-Sharing Ratios is critical for several reasons:

shariahCompliance.title: Shariah Compliance
shariahCompliance.description: Islamic law requires full transparency in contracts. Hidden terms or ambiguity (gharar) render a contract invalid.

customerTrust.title: Customer Trust
customerTrust.description: Clear PSR disclosure builds confidence that the bank is operating ethically and sharing profits fairly.

regulatoryCompliance.title: Regulatory Compliance
regulatoryCompliance.description: AAOIFI standards (FAS 6, FAS 11) mandate explicit PSR disclosure in financial statements and customer-facing materials.

informedDecisions.title: Informed Decision-Making
informedDecisions.description: Customers need to understand how returns are calculated to compare Islamic investment accounts with conventional alternatives.

aaoifiRequirements.title: AAOIFI Disclosure Requirements
aaoifiRequirements.intro: The Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) has established clear guidelines for PSR disclosure:

fas6.title: FAS 6: Equity of Investment Account Holders
fas6.intro: AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standard No. 6 requires:

precontractual.label: Pre-contractual disclosure:
precontractual.text: The PSR must be communicated to customers before they open an investment account.

written.label: Written documentation:
written.text: The PSR must appear in the account opening agreement.

methodology.label: Profit calculation methodology:
methodology.text: Banks must explain how profits are calculated and allocated.

loss.label: Loss-bearing disclosure:
loss.text: Customers must be informed that losses (if any) are borne entirely by them, while the bank loses only its time and effort.

fas11.title: FAS 11: Provisions and Reserves
fas11.intro: This standard addresses how banks handle Profit Equalization Reserves (PER) and Investment Risk Reserves (IRR):

per.label: PER:
per.text: Amounts set aside to smooth profit distribution across periods (disclosed separately)

irr.label: IRR:
irr.text: Reserves to cover potential investment losses (also disclosed separately)

transparency.label: Transparency requirement:
transparency.text: Customers must understand how reserves impact their actual profit share

requirements.percentage: The PSR must be expressed as a percentage of profits, not a fixed amount
requirements.agreement: Both parties must agree to the PSR at the contract's inception
requirements.tiered: The PSR can be tiered (different ratios for different profit levels) if clearly disclosed
requirements.changes: Any changes to the PSR require customer consent and cannot apply retroactively

bestPractices.title: Disclosure Best Practices
bestPractices.intro: Beyond meeting minimum AAOIFI requirements, Islamic financial institutions should adopt these best practices:

marketing.label: Marketing materials:
marketing.text: Include PSR ranges in brochures, websites, and advertisements

accountOpening.label: Account opening:
accountOpening.text: Highlight the PSR prominently in the application form

welcomeKits.label: Welcome kits:
welcomeKits.text: Provide a one-page PSR explainer to new customers

statements.label: Quarterly statements:
statements.text: Recap the PSR and show actual profit allocation

plainLanguage.title: 2. Plain Language
plainLanguage.badExample: "The mudarib shall retain 35% of realized profits from the commingled investment pool, subject to PER and IRR appropriations as determined by the ACE."
plainLanguage.goodExample: "When your investment earns a profit, you receive 65% and the bank receives 35%. Any profits set aside for reserves will be explained in your quarterly statement."

visualAids.title: 3. Visual Aids
visualAids.intro: Use charts, infographics, and examples to illustrate PSR:
visualAids.exampleNote: If the bank earns 1,000,000 units in profit from your investment, you receive 700,000 units and the bank receives 300,000 units.

comparativeContext.title: 4. Comparative Context
comparativeContext.intro: Help customers understand PSR by comparing it to conventional interest:

conventional.label: Conventional savings account:
conventional.text: 2% fixed interest (guaranteed, regardless of bank performance)

islamic.label: Islamic Mudarabah account:
islamic.text: 70% of profits (variable, based on actual investment returns)

comparativeContext.clarification: Clarify that if the bank earns higher returns in Islamic investing, the customer's PSR-based returns may exceed conventional interest but there's also downside risk.

calculationExamples.title: PSR Calculation Examples
calculationExamples.intro: Let's walk through practical scenarios to demonstrate how PSR works:

scenario1.title: Scenario 1: Simple Profit Distribution
scenario1.setupDetail: A customer deposits 10,000,000 units into a Mudarabah investment account with a PSR of 60:40 (60% customer, 40% bank).
scenario1.performanceDetail: The bank invests the funds and earns 800,000 units in profit over the year.
scenario1.effectiveReturn: Effective return for the customer: 4.8% (480K profit ÷ 10M deposit)

scenario2.title: Scenario 2: Loss Scenario
scenario2.setupDetail: Same customer, same 10,000,000 units deposit, PSR 60:40.
scenario2.performanceDetail: The bank's investments perform poorly, resulting in a 300,000 units loss.
scenario2.keyPrincipleText: In Mudarabah, capital losses are borne entirely by the capital provider (customer), while the fund manager (bank) loses only its time and effort unless the loss resulted from negligence or breach of contract.

scenario3.title: Scenario 3: Tiered PSR
scenario3.intro: Some banks use tiered PSR structures to incentivize higher performance:
scenario3.note: This structure rewards the bank for generating higher returns while still ensuring customers receive the majority of profits at all levels.

commonMistakes.title: Common PSR Disclosure Mistakes
commonMistakes.intro: Avoid these frequent errors that can lead to Shariah non-compliance or customer confusion:

mistake1.title: Using Fixed Amounts Instead of Percentages
mistake1.why: PSR must be expressed as a percentage of profits, not a fixed currency amount. Saying "the bank gets 100,000 units" violates Mudarabah principles.
mistake1.fix: Always use percentages: "the bank receives 30% of profits."

mistake2.title: Hidden or Buried Disclosure
mistake2.why: Putting PSR in fine print or deep in contract appendices undermines transparency.
mistake2.fix: Feature PSR prominently on page 1 of account agreements and marketing materials.

mistake3.title: Ambiguous Loss-Sharing Terms
mistake3.why: Failing to clarify that customers bear capital losses (while banks bear effort losses) creates false expectations.
mistake3.fix: Explicitly state: "You receive [X]% of profits. In case of losses, your capital may decrease, but the bank does not receive any profit."

mistake4.title: Comparing PSR Directly to Interest Rates
mistake4.why: Saying "Our 60% PSR is like 4% interest" is misleading because PSR returns vary based on performance.
mistake4.fix: Provide historical examples: "Over the past year, our 60% PSR resulted in an average return of 4.2%, compared to 3.5% conventional interest."

mistake5.title: Changing PSR Without Customer Consent
mistake5.why: Unilateral changes to PSR violate the mutuality principle of Islamic contracts.
mistake5.fix: Any PSR adjustments require written customer agreement and cannot apply to existing deposits retroactively.

regulatoryContext.title: Regulatory Compliance & PSR
regulatoryContext.intro: Disclosure requirements for Profit-Sharing Ratios must satisfy both regional business standards and local central bank guidelines.

aaoifi.label: AAOIFI for Shariah:
aaoifi.text: Follow FAS 6 and FAS 11 standards for pre-contractual and financial statement disclosure of PSR.

centralBank.label: Central Bank Supervision:
centralBank.text: Report Mudarabah accounts properly to central banks (e.g. as "investment deposits" under CBN guidelines in Nigeria or "participation accounts" under COBAC in Central Africa).

ohada.label: OHADA Chart of Accounts:
ohada.text: In OHADA-zone countries (West and Central Africa), map the dual-ledger structures carefully to reflect investment pool returns.

languageAdaptations.title: Language & Regional Adaptations
languageAdaptations.intro: Depending on the jurisdiction, documentation must align with official languages and terminology:

francophone.label: Francophone Regions (CEMAC, WAEMU):
francophone.text: Translate key terms accurately in French, e.g., Ratio de Partage des Bénéfices (RPB) for PSR.

anglophone.label: Anglophone Regions (Nigeria):
anglophone.text: Use terms standardized by local non-interest banking circulars.

reportingRequirements.title: Regulatory Reporting Requirements
reportingRequirements.intro: Quarterly reports submitted to central banks should generally disclose:

items.ranges: Aggregate PSR ranges across account types
items.allocation: Actual profit/loss allocation paid out to depositors
items.reserves: Reserves (PER/IRR) held on behalf of investment account holders

customerEducation.title: Customer Education Strategies
customerEducation.intro: Beyond disclosure, proactive education helps customers understand and appreciate PSR:

workshops.title: 1. Onboarding Workshops
workshops.intro: Host monthly sessions at branch locations explaining:

items.difference: How Mudarabah accounts differ from conventional savings
items.fluctuation: Why PSR fluctuates based on investment performance
items.statements: How to read quarterly profit distribution statements

calculator.label: PSR calculator:
calculator.text: Customers input their deposit amount and estimated return to see projected profit splits

faq.label: FAQ section:
faq.text: Address common questions like "Can PSR change?" and "What if the bank loses money?"

items.totalProfits: Total profits earned by the bank from customer's investment

introduction.leadParagraph: Islamic financial institutions operating in OHADA member states face a unique challenge: they must comply with both AAOIFI Islamic accounting standards and OHADA regional accounting regulations. This dual compliance framework requires careful reconciliation to satisfy Shariah boards, regulators, and stakeholders.
introduction.paragraph2: This article provides a comprehensive guide to understanding the differences between these two frameworks and implementing practical strategies to meet both sets of requirements simultaneously.

regulatory.label: Regulatory compliance:
regulatory.text: Regional central banks require OHADA-compliant reporting

stakeholder.label: Stakeholder confidence:
stakeholder.text: Transparent reporting builds trust with investors and customers

efficiency.label: Operational efficiency:

aaoifiOverview.title: What is AAOIFI?
aaoifiOverview.intro: The Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) is an international Islamic finance standard-setting body established in 1990 in Bahrain.

scope.title: Scope of AAOIFI Standards
scope.intro: AAOIFI issues standards across four domains:

fas.label: Financial Accounting Standards (FAS):
fas.text: 30+ standards covering Islamic transaction recognition, measurement, and disclosure

ss.label: Shariah Standards (SS):
ss.text: Guidelines on Islamic product structures and contracts

gs.label: Governance Standards (GS):
gs.text: Corporate governance and Shariah board requirements

as.label: Audit Standards (AS):
as.text: Auditing procedures specific to Islamic institutions

substance.label: Substance over form:
substance.text: Economic reality takes precedence over legal form

shariah.label: Shariah compliance:
shariah.text: All transactions must align with Islamic law

transparency.label: Transparency:
transparency.text: Full disclosure of profit-sharing ratios, investment risks, and Shariah approval

stakeholder.label: Stakeholder protection:
stakeholder.text: Special attention to Investment Account Holders (IAH) rights

adoption.title: Adoption Status
adoption.text: AAOIFI standards are mandatory in Bahrain, Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar, Sudan, and Syria. They are recommended or partially adopted in over 45 countries, including many African nations developing Islamic finance sectors.

ohadaOverview.title: What is OHADA?
ohadaOverview.intro: The Organisation pour l'Harmonisation en Afrique du Droit des Affaires (OHADA) is a system harmonizing business law across 17 West and Central African countries, including both CEMAC and WAEMU member states.

framework.title: OHADA Accounting Framework
framework.intro: OHADA's Uniform Act on Accounting and Financial Reporting standardizes:

formats.label: Financial statement formats:
formats.text: Balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement, and notes

principles.label: Accounting principles:
principles.text: Accrual basis, going concern, consistency, prudence

application.title: OHADA & Central Bank Application
application.intro: In member countries across West and Central Africa, regional banking regulators (such as COBAC for CEMAC or BCEAO for WAEMU) require all financial institutions to:

items.quarterly: Submit quarterly financial statements in OHADA format

keyDifferences.title: Key Differences Between AAOIFI and OHADA
keyDifferences.intro: While both frameworks aim for transparency and consistency, they differ significantly:

chartOfAccounts.title: Chart of Accounts Mapping
chartOfAccounts.intro: One of the most critical reconciliation tasks is mapping Islamic finance transactions to OHADA's SYSCOHADA chart of accounts:

syscohada.title: SYSCOHADA Structure
syscohada.intro: OHADA uses an 8-class chart of accounts:

murabaha.title: Murabaha Receivables
murabaha.note: Record Murabaha receivables under customer accounts, with subledger detail indicating Islamic product type.

mudarabah.title: Mudarabah Investment Accounts
mudarabah.note: OHADA requires on-balance sheet treatment, but notes can clarify the Mudarabah nature and PSR arrangement.

profitDistribution.title: Profit Distribution to IAH
profitDistribution.note: While economically profit-sharing, OHADA treats it as interest expense. Detailed notes must clarify the Shariah-compliant nature.

zakat.title: Zakat
zakat.note: Zakat is treated as a charitable expense. If the institution facilitates Zakat payment for customers, use Class 4 (payables).

financialStatements.title: Financial Statement Requirements
financialStatements.intro: Both AAOIFI and OHADA mandate specific financial statement formats:

items.incomeStatement: Statement of Income: Separates shareholder income from IAH income
items.restrictedInvestments: Statement of Changes in Restricted Investments: For Mudarabah accounts
items.zakatFunds: Statement of Sources and Uses of Zakat and Charity Funds
items.notes: Notes to Financial Statements: Including PSR disclosures and Shariah board report

items.incomeStatement: Income Statement (Compte de Résultat): Detailed revenue and expense breakdown
items.cashFlows: Cash Flow Statement (Tableau de Flux de Trésorerie)
items.notes: Notes (Annexe): Accounting policies and detailed disclosures

aaoifiBooks.label: Maintain books in AAOIFI format:
aaoifiBooks.text: This ensures Shariah compliance and provides detailed Islamic finance tracking

mappingRules.label: Create OHADA mapping rules:
mappingRules.text: Define how each AAOIFI account maps to SYSCOHADA

ohadaStatements.label: Generate OHADA statements:
ohadaStatements.text: Use mapping rules to produce regulatory-compliant reports

notesSupplement.label: Supplement with notes:
notesSupplement.text: Provide extensive footnotes explaining Islamic finance structures within OHADA reports

dualCompliance.title: Dual Compliance Strategy
dualCompliance.intro: Implementing both frameworks simultaneously requires a systematic approach:

step1.title: Step 1: Establish Parallel Chart of Accounts
step1.intro: Create a dual chart of accounts where each AAOIFI account has a corresponding SYSCOHADA code:

step2.title: Step 2: Implement Subledgers
step2.intro: Use subledgers to capture Islamic-specific details while maintaining OHADA compliance:

customer.label: Customer subledger:
customer.text: Track Murabaha contract details (cost, markup, installment schedule)

investment.label: Investment account subledger:
investment.text: Record PSR, profit allocation, and IAH balances

shariah.label: Shariah compliance subledger:
shariah.text: Document Shariah board approvals and audit findings

steps.step2: Run automated mapping: Convert AAOIFI balances to SYSCOHADA accounts
steps.step3: Generate OHADA statements: Produce balance sheet, income statement, and notes
steps.step4: Perform variance analysis: Verify that AAOIFI and OHADA reports reconcile
steps.step5: Submit to Regulator: File OHADA-compliant reports with your central bank (such as COBAC or BCEAO)
steps.step6: Prepare AAOIFI report for Shariah board: Provide Islamic finance-specific analysis

step4.title: Step 4: Disclosure Notes
step4.intro: Use OHADA financial statement notes (Annexe) to bridge the gap:

note1.label: Note 1 - Accounting policies:
note1.text: Explain that the institution operates under dual compliance (AAOIFI + OHADA)

note2.label: Note 2 - Islamic products:
note2.text: Define Murabaha, Mudarabah, Musharakah, and their economic substance

note3.label: Note 3 - Investment accounts:
note3.text: Disclose PSR, profit distribution methodology, and IAH rights

note4.label: Note 4 - Shariah compliance:
note4.text: Reference Shariah board composition and approval process

note5.label: Note 5 - Zakat:
note5.text: Explain Zakat calculation and distribution if applicable

practicalImplementation.title: Practical Implementation Tips
practicalImplementation.intro: Based on real-world experience from Islamic finance institutions operating in OHADA zones:

tip1.title: 1. Start with Core Products
tip1.intro: Don't try to map every Islamic product at once. Begin with:

products.murabaha: Murabaha (easiest to map to conventional loan accounting)
products.mudarabah: Mudarabah investment accounts (similar to term deposits)

tip1.complexProducts: Add complex products (Musharakah, Ijara, Salam) gradually as you refine your mapping rules.

tip2.title: 2. Engage Both AAOIFI and OHADA Experts

aaoifiExpert.label: Hire an AAOIFI-certified accountant:
aaoifiExpert.text: Ensure someone on your team understands Islamic finance accounting principles

ohadaPractitioner.text: Work with accountants experienced in regional regulatory reporting

shariahCoordination.text: Ensure accounting treatments align with Shariah interpretations

tip3.title: 3. Build Audit Trails

items.mappingRationale: Why a particular AAOIFI account maps to a specific SYSCOHADA code

tip3.conclusion: This documentation protects against regulatory scrutiny and simplifies annual audits.

section1.title: 1. About this policy
section1.paragraph1: This privacy policy explains how TIKARI Technology Limited ("TIKARI", "we", "us") collects, uses, discloses, and protects information about you when you visit tikari.cm or enquire about our platform. It does not cover data processed within the TIKARI platform on behalf of our institutional customers, which is governed by our Data Processing Agreement with each customer institution.
section1.paragraph2: Our operations comply with Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on cybersecurity and cybercrime in Cameroon, supervised by ANTIC (National Agency for Information and Communication Technologies), and relevant COBAC guidelines on banking secrecy and customer data protection.

section2.title: 2. Information we collect
section2.paragraph1: From website visitors: We collect information you provide when you submit our demo request form, including name, work email address, institution name, role, and any message you include. We may also collect standard web server logs (IP address, browser type, pages visited) for security and analytics purposes.
section2.paragraph2: We do not: use third-party advertising trackers, sell your information to third parties, or send unsolicited marketing emails to people who have not opted in.

section3.title: 3. How we use your information
section3.intro: When you submit a demo request, we use your information to:

items.item1: Contact you to schedule the requested demo
items.item2: Tailor the demo to your institution type and stated questions
items.item3: Send follow-up information related to TIKARI that you have requested

section3.outro: We do not add you to a bulk marketing mailing list without explicit consent.

section4.title: 4. Data retention
section4.content: Demo enquiry data is retained for 24 months from the date of submission, or until you request deletion. We delete data on request. You may contact us at hi@instanvi.com.

section5.title: 5. Data security
section5.content: We use encryption in transit (HTTPS/TLS) for all web communications. Form submission data is stored in access-controlled systems available only to the TIKARI team. We do not store payment card data. No payment is collected on this website.

section6.title: 6. Third-party services
section6.content: Our website may use third-party services for hosting and basic analytics. These services are bound by their own privacy policies and are not permitted to use data about visitors to our site for their own advertising purposes.

section7.title: 7. Your rights
section7.content: You have the right to request access to, correction of, or deletion of any personal information we hold about you under regional CEMAC consumer safety guidelines. To exercise any of these rights, contact us at hi@instanvi.com. We will respond within 30 days.

section8.title: 8. Changes to this policy
section8.content: We may update this policy from time to time. The date at the top of this page indicates when it was last revised. Continued use of the website following an update constitutes acceptance of the revised policy.
